title: NASA's GIMLI Mission Will Probe Beneath a Giant Pit on the Moon
excerpt: The Planetary Science Institute-led payload will use radar, seismic sensors and gravity measurements to test whether the Marius Hills Pit opens into a lava tube that could shelter astronauts.
body:
• NASA has selected GIMLI, a Planetary Science Institute-led payload, to investigate whether the Marius Hills Pit on the Moon opens into a large underground lava tube.
  • Carried by a commercial lander and rover, GIMLI will combine ground-penetrating radar, active-source seismic sensors, a gravimeter and cameras to map what lies beneath the pit.
  • A confirmed lava tube could shelter future astronauts from radiation, micrometeoroids and extreme temperature swings, and would record the Moon's ancient volcanic history.
  • NASA announced the selection on September 30, 2026, through its PRISM program. No launch date or delivery provider has been announced.

NASA has selected a mission to investigate what lies beneath a giant hole on the Moon. The Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation, or GIMLI, will be deployed at the Marius Hills Pit to test whether the opening leads into a large underground lava tube, NASA said in its September 30 announcement. The payload is led by the Planetary Science Institute (PSI) and was selected through the agency's Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program.

The Marius Hills Pit is a steep-sided opening about 65 by 90 metres (213 by 295 feet) in Oceanus Procellarum, one of the Moon's most volcanically varied regions, according to Astronomy. EarthSky puts the pit at about 90 metres across and roughly 50 metres deep. Scientists believe it may be a skylight, a place where the roof of a lava tube collapsed. It is one of nearly 300 pits identified on the lunar surface.

How GIMLI Will Look Underground

GIMLI will not enter the pit. Instead, a lander and rover delivered through NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative will carry its instruments around the opening. Ground-penetrating radar supplied by the Norwegian Space Agency will probe buried structures with radio waves, seismic sensors will record how deliberately generated vibrations travel through the ground, and a gravimeter will measure local gravity for signs of missing mass where an empty chamber might sit. Cameras will image the surface and the pit walls, according to SciTechDaily.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=QcNdYZeFBto

""Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the Moon," said Gareth Morgan, PSI senior scientist and GIMLI's deputy principal investigator."

"It's long been a desire of mine to reintroduce intentional active-source seismic methods to planetary science, as it has essentially not been done since the Apollo astronauts conducted the first seismic surveys on the Moon," said GIMLI leader Than Putzig, PSI associate director and senior scientist. Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, will build much of the equipment and integrate the instruments onto the lander and rover. Co-investigators come from Boise State University, Johns Hopkins University, the Lunar and Planetary Institute and the University of Oslo.

Why a Lunar Cave Matters

Orbital observations have given scientists reason to think a void is there. A 2017 study paired radar data from Japan's Kaguya orbiter with gravity measurements from NASA's GRAIL mission and found strong evidence of empty space beneath the surface around the Marius Hills Pit. In 2024, radar data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter suggested a pit in Mare Tranquillitatis might lead to an underground cavern about 100 feet long. Lava tubes form when the surface of a lava flow cools while molten rock keeps moving beneath it, then drains away. On Earth such tubes reach about 30 metres across; under the Moon's weaker gravity, studies suggest they could reach 385 metres.

If GIMLI confirms a substantial tube, the payoff runs in two directions. Underground spaces could offer future astronauts ready-made protection from extreme temperatures, harmful radiation and micrometeoroid bombardment, NASA said. For scientists, the tube and the pit's exposed walls, which show layers of lava flows and regolith normally hidden underground, would preserve a record of how volcanism built the lunar surface. "Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the Moon," said Gareth Morgan, PSI senior scientist and GIMLI's deputy principal investigator.

Part of a Wider Moon Base Push

GIMLI was one of three PRISM selections NASA announced on September 30, alongside the Lunar Environment Monitoring Station – South Pole, a long-term hazard monitor led by Mehdi Benna of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, and DISCO, which will measure ice in lunar micro-cold traps under Ariel Deutsch of NASA's Ames Research Center. "These PRISM selections will directly help NASA minimize risks to our astronauts while maximizing our agency goals as we set up humanity's first lunar outpost in preparation for sending the first astronauts to Mars," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate.

The mission, named after Gimli, the cave-loving dwarf in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, has no announced launch date. Even a negative result would not end the inquiry: if no cave is found, GIMLI's measurements would still show how the pit formed and clarify the volcanic history of the site, according to EarthSky.
